newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council readies first vote on top U.N. post.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council readies first vote on top U.N. post.

text.p: The Security Council on Tuesday conducts its first unofficial poll for the post of U.N. secretary-general with four African candidates vying for Boutros Boutros-Ghali's job.
Diplomats said there would be at least two rounds in what Council President Paolo Fulci of Italy termed an informal straw poll on four names submitted on Friday.

Boutros-Ghali, vetoed by the United States, temporarily suspended his candidacy last week but did not withdraw from the race. His name is not expected to be put in nomination again unless there is a deadlock.

The new candidtes are: Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping; Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of Islamic Conference; Amara Essy, foreign minister of the Ivory Coast; and Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, the former U.N. special envoy for Burundi who is executive secretary of the Washington-based Global Coalition for Africa.

To win, a candidate needs at least nine votes in the 15-seat council and no veto from any of its five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. Any candidate approved by the council must be endorsed by the 185-member General Assembly before December 31 when Boutros-Ghali's five-year term expires.
But in the Byzantine U.N. procedures, members can vote for more than one candidate and a veto does not necessarily preclude another vote -- and another veto -- on the same candidate.

According to envoys at the council's closed-door meeting on Monday, the five permanent members are to receive specially marked ballots after the first round of informal voting to see if any vetos emerge.
But it is unclear whether the vote will be an indicator of which candidate is ahead or will only winnow out the weaker candidates.
In 1991, when Boutros-Ghali, then Egypt's deputy prime minister, a professor, author and authority on international law, was elected, no permanent member used a veto in any of the balloting.
But this year's contest may be fierce with vetoes anticipated in reaction to the U.S. veto against Boutros-Ghali on Nov. 19 when the other 14 council members supported him.

The contest has already turned into a language war with South African President Nelson Mandela revealing on Sunday that French President Jacques Chirac would veto Salim A. Salim, the skilled secretary-general of the Organisation of Africa Unity, for not speaking fluent French.

Salim's name was not submitted on Monday as diplomats had expected. Also missing from Monday's list was Senegalese Foreign Minister Moustapha Niasse, expected to draw a veto from China because of his country's ties with Taiwan.

All four candidates before the council speak French and all have extensive experience in foreign affairs. But it is not known whether France would veto Annan, the only nominee from an "anglophone" country.
Both Boutros-Ghali and his predecessor, Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, were more proficient in French than in English.

The council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.
